title: The Art of Banarasi Weaving — 15 Centuries of Brocade
excerpt: Discover the ancient tradition of Banarasi brocade weaving — from the pit looms of Varanasi to the hands of master craftsmen who have kept this art alive for over fifteen centuries.
body:
Deep inside the ancient lanes of Varanasi — in neighbourhoods called *mohallas* that have not changed in centuries — something extraordinary happens every morning. A master weaver, or *karigar*, descends to his pit loom and begins work. A shuttle of pure gold *zari* passes between warp threads of shimmering Katan silk. One row at a time, a motif takes shape: a lotus, a mango, a peacock. This is the art of Banarasi brocade — practised here for over fifteen hundred years.

## Origins — From Varanasi's Ancient Looms

The history of Banarasi silk is inseparable from the history of Varanasi itself, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth. Sanskrit texts from the 3rd century BCE describe fine silk weaving in this region as *kashi-vastra* — cloth of Kashi. By the Mughal period, the art had reached its zenith. Emperor Akbar's court demanded brocades woven with real gold and silver, and the karigar communities of Varanasi responded with an artistry that still astonishes today.

The Mughal influence permanently shaped the visual vocabulary of Banarasi design. The characteristic motifs — the *kalga* (paisley), the *jaal* (flowing lattice), the *butti* (scattered flower), and elaborate floral jalis — all carry the imprint of Mughal miniature painting. What the court commissioned as fabric, the weavers turned into art.

![A Banarasi Katan silk saree with gold zari brocade](https://ik.imagekit.io/Amayaa2026/blog/BLG-001.jpg?tr=f-auto,q-85)

## How a Banarasi Saree is Made

The process begins not at the loom but in the dyeing vats. Silk yarn — imported from Bangalore for Katan work — is mordanted and dyed in precisely calculated shades. The colour must penetrate fully, because a Banarasi saree is expected to outlast generations.

### The Pit Loom

The traditional Banarasi loom, called a *khaddi*, is set into a pit dug in the workshop floor. The weaver sits at ground level, legs dangling below, passing the shuttle with a precision built from decades of practice. The *draw boy* — historically a young apprentice — pulls pattern cords from above, a system that predates the Jacquard mechanism by centuries.

Today many workshops use a Jacquard head, a punched-card system that translates a design into a precise sequence of thread lifts. But the loom itself has barely changed in five hundred years.

### Zari — The Thread of Gold

The defining element of Banarasi brocade is *zari*: metallic thread. Traditional *real zari* used fine silver wire wrapped around a silk core, then plated with gold. Today most production uses *tested zari* (silver-plated) or *imitation zari* (copper-cored). The finest pieces — like those carried by Amayaa — use high-quality tested zari that catches light with unmistakable warmth.

> "Each border of a heavy Banarasi Kadwa takes forty days of work. My father did it. His father before him. We do not count the hours. We count the rows."
>
> — *Mohammad Iqbal Ansari, master karigar, Varanasi — third generation*

### The Four Banarasi Weave Families

Not all Banarasi silk is the same. The tradition encompasses four distinct weave structures:

- **Katan** — Pure silk warp and weft with zari brocade as a supplementary element. The most prestigious variety. Heavy, luminous, and extraordinarily durable.
- **Organza (Kora)** — Sheer, crisp silk made from undegummed raw silk. The fabric holds its own structure, giving a floating quality to the zari work.
- **Georgette** — A crinkle-weave silk, softer and more fluid. Zari appears as delicate scattered motifs across the surface.
- **Shattir** — Satin-based weave, intensely lustrous. The preferred choice for heavy bridal wear and high-occasion draping.

## The GI Tag and Why It Matters

In 2009, Banarasi silk received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag — the same legal protection that governs Champagne, Darjeeling tea, and Scotch whisky. A genuine Banarasi saree can only be produced within the Varanasi cluster, which includes the districts of Bhadohi and Mirzapur. This tag protects weavers from the flood of power-loom imitations sold across India.

When you acquire a Banarasi saree through Amayaa, it comes with documentation from the karigar family — the weaver's name, their village, the weave structure, and the zari grade. We believe the maker deserves recognition as much as the making does.

## How to Identify a Genuine Handloom Banarasi

Four reliable indicators before you buy:

1. **Reverse side** — floating zari threads are visible where the brocade pattern is formed. The hallmark of authentic supplementary weft work.
2. **Raised border** — run your finger along the zari border. It should feel gently raised, not flat.
3. **Light test** — hold the saree up to light. Genuine Katan silk is semi-transparent, with the pattern visible from both sides.
4. **Selvedge finish** — the side edge is finished naturally from the loom, not cut and overstitched.

---

## Caring for Your Banarasi

A Banarasi silk saree is a living heirloom. With the right care, it will outlast you.

- **Dry clean only.** Never machine wash. Water causes zari to oxidise and lose its lustre permanently.
- **Store in muslin, not plastic.** Silk must breathe. Plastic traps moisture and causes irreversible yellowing.
- **Refold every six months.** Permanent fold lines weaken silk fibres. Change the fold positions periodically.
- **Keep away from direct light.** UV exposure degrades both silk and zari. Store in a dark drawer or inside a cotton cloth bag.

---

*At Amayaa, every Banarasi saree is sourced directly from karigar families in Varanasi. We visit the workshops, watch the weaving, and bring back only pieces we would wear ourselves.*

[Explore our Banarasi collection →](amayaa_sarees.html?region=Banarasi)

title: Tussar vs Kosa Silk — Understanding India's Wild Silks
excerpt: Tussar and Kosa are India's two great wild silks — spun not in captivity but in the forests of Jharkhand, Bihar and Chhattisgarh. Understanding the difference transforms how you shop for silk.
body:
India produces more varieties of silk than any country on earth. Among them, Tussar and Kosa stand apart — not because of their lustre or weight, but because of where they come from: the wild forests of central and eastern India, untouched by sericulture farms.

## What Is Wild Silk?

Most silk — Mulberry silk, Kanjivaram, Banarasi — comes from the domesticated silkworm *Bombyx mori*, reared on mulberry leaves in controlled conditions. Wild silks are different. They are spun by silkworms that live freely in forest trees, feed on wild leaves, and produce a coarser, more textured thread as a result.

That texture is not a flaw. It is the signature.

## Tussar Silk — The Gold of the Forests

Tussar (also spelled Tasar) is produced primarily by the silkworm *Antheraea mylitta*, which feeds on Asan, Arjun, and Sal trees. It is most abundantly produced in Jharkhand, Bihar, and West Bengal — states where forest cover and tribal weaver communities have coexisted for centuries.

**Characteristics of Tussar:**
- Rich golden-brown natural colour — from pale champagne to deep amber
- Coarser texture with a distinctive slub (uneven thread thickness)
- Lower sheen than mulberry silk, but a warm, earthy glow
- Naturally breathable and ideal for both formal and everyday wear
- Holds natural and vegetable dyes exceptionally well

Tussar silk has been awarded the Geographical Indication (GI) tag in multiple producing states. The Office of the Development Commissioner for Handlooms, Government of India, recognises Bhagalpur Silk (Bihar) and Jharkhand Tasar as protected designations.

> *"Tussar is the democracy of silks — it is worn by queens and weavers alike."* — a common saying among Bhagalpur weavers

## Kosa Silk — Chhattisgarh's Quiet Treasure

Kosa silk is produced by the silkworm *Antheraea paphia*, which feeds almost exclusively on Sal (*Shorea robusta*) leaves in the forests of Chhattisgarh — particularly around Champa, Raigarh, and Bilaspur.

Kosa is rarer than Tussar and considerably finer. The thread is slightly smoother, the colour more ivory than gold, and the fabric drapes with a fluidity that surprises first-time buyers.

**Characteristics of Kosa:**
- Ivory to pale gold natural colour — more uniform than Tussar
- Smoother hand-feel, though still distinctly different from mulberry silk
- Subtle sheen — understated and sophisticated
- Strong and durable — many Kosa sarees last multiple generations
- Produced almost entirely by tribal artisan cooperatives in Chhattisgarh

The state government of Chhattisgarh actively promotes Kosa through its weaver cooperative programmes, and the fabric holds GI protection under the Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999 (GI Application No. 62).

## Tussar vs Kosa — A Quick Comparison

| | Tussar | Kosa |
|---|---|---|
| **Silkworm** | *Antheraea mylitta* | *Antheraea paphia* |
| **Primary states** | Jharkhand, Bihar, WB | Chhattisgarh |
| **Colour** | Golden to amber | Ivory to pale gold |
| **Texture** | Coarser, visible slub | Smoother, finer |
| **Sheen** | Warm, earthy | Subtle, understated |
| **GI Protected** | Yes (multiple states) | Yes |

## How to Identify Authentic Wild Silk

1. **Look for the slub** — authentic wild silk will show slight irregularities in the weave. Perfectly uniform threads indicate machine-processed or blended fabric.
2. **Check the colour** — natural Tussar and Kosa are never brilliant white. If it looks bleached white, it has been processed.
3. **The burn test** — real silk burns slowly, smells like burnt hair, and leaves a crushable ash. Synthetic silk melts and smells of plastic.
4. **Ask for the Silk Mark** — the Silk Mark Organisation of India certifies and labels authentic silk products. Look for the tag.

## Why They Matter

Tussar and Kosa are not just fabrics. They are the livelihoods of hundreds of thousands of tribal weavers — communities in Jharkhand, Bihar, and Chhattisgarh for whom silk rearing and weaving is an inherited vocation. Choosing authentic wild silk over imitations is a direct act of support for these communities.

At Amayaa by Polka Dots, every wild silk saree we carry is verified for origin and authenticity. When you wear Tussar or Kosa, you carry the forest with you.

---

*Content references: Office of the Development Commissioner for Handlooms, Ministry of Textiles, Government of India (handlooms.gov.in); Silk Mark Organisation of India (silkmarkindia.com); Geographical Indications Registry, Government of India (ipindia.gov.in); Chhattisgarh Hastshilp Vikas Board.*

title: The Weavers of Bishnupur — Keepers of the Baluchari Tradition
excerpt: Baluchari silk from Bishnupur, West Bengal, is one of India's most literary weaves — each pallu a tapestry of Puranic narratives woven in silk. Here is the story of the weavers keeping it alive.
body:
There are sarees that drape beautifully. And then there are sarees that tell stories.

The Baluchari silk of Bishnupur, West Bengal, belongs firmly to the second category. Woven on the flat, terracotta-red plains of Bankura district, Baluchari sarees use silk brocade not for geometric patterns or floral motifs, but to depict scenes from the Mahabharata and Ramayana — on the pallu, on the border, across every inch of the anchal.

To wear a Baluchari is to wear a story.

## Origins — A Craft Born Under Mughal Influence

The Baluchari tradition traces its origins to the 18th century, when the craft flourished in the village of Baluchar, near Murshidabad — then the seat of the Nawabs of Bengal. Under Nawabi patronage, weavers from this region developed an extraordinary vocabulary of narrative motifs: courtly scenes, Europeans in coaches, hookah-smoking nawabs, and figures from the epics.

When the Nawabi court declined in the early 19th century, the craft migrated to Bishnupur — a town already famous for its terracotta temples and its history as the capital of the Malla kings, who were great patrons of the arts.

## The Near-Extinction and the Revival

By the mid-20th century, Baluchari was nearly extinct. Power looms had undercut the market, the elaborate drawloom technique was being forgotten, and the weaver community had dwindled to a handful of families.

The revival is credited largely to **Subho Tagore** — a textile expert and grandson of Rabindranath Tagore's circle — who worked with the surviving weaver families in the 1950s to document the motifs, revive the drawloom technique, and reconnect the craft with its markets. The West Bengal government and the Handicrafts Board subsequently took up the cause.

Today, Bishnupur's Baluchari is protected under the Geographical Indications of Goods Act, with GI Tag No. 90 for "Baluchari Saree" — one of the first GI tags awarded to a textile in India.

## The Weave — How It Is Made

Baluchari is woven on a traditional jacquard or drawloom. The weaver works with pure mulberry silk — the warp threads in one colour, the weft brocade in another, with the narrative motifs created by supplementary silk weft threads.

The pallu (the trailing end of the saree that falls over the shoulder) is the centrepiece: typically depicting a scene from the Mahabharata or Ramayana, framed by intricate borders of smaller motifs.

A single Baluchari saree takes **3 to 5 days** to weave. Complex pallus with multiple figures can take up to two weeks.

**Common motifs include:**
- Scenes from the Kurukshetra war (Mahabharata)
- The chariot of Arjuna driven by Lord Krishna
- Scenes from the Ramayana — Sita's abduction, Ram's court
- Courtly figures — nawabs, palanquins, hookah bearers
- Kalka (paisley) and floral scrollwork borders

## The Weavers of Bishnupur Today

The weaver community in and around Bishnupur — primarily from the Tanti community — numbers in the hundreds of families. Most work from home on pit looms that have been in their families for generations.

The **Bishnupur Tantubay Samabay Samity** (Weavers' Cooperative Society) plays a central role in providing raw material, design support, and market access. The West Bengal Khadi and Village Industries Board and the National Handloom Development Corporation also support the weaver community.

> *"We do not just weave threads. We weave the epics. When someone wears our pallu, they are carrying the Mahabharata on their shoulder."* — Baluchari weaver, Bishnupur

## How to Identify Authentic Baluchari

1. **The pallu narrative** — authentic Baluchari will have clearly identifiable figures from Indian mythology on the pallu, not abstract motifs.
2. **Pure silk** — the fabric should have the characteristic weight and drape of mulberry silk. Request a Silk Mark certificate.
3. **GI Tag** — look for the GI certification label. Authentic Bishnupur Baluchari carries GI Tag No. 90.
4. **The weaver's signature** — some weavers include a small self-portrait motif in a corner of the pallu — a centuries-old tradition.

## Caring for Your Baluchari

Baluchari sarees should be dry cleaned. Fold them along the motif lines to avoid crease lines forming across the faces of figures. Store with muslin, never plastic.

---

*Content references: Geographical Indications Registry, Government of India — GI Tag No. 90, "Baluchari Saree" (ipindia.gov.in); Office of the Development Commissioner for Handlooms, Ministry of Textiles (handlooms.gov.in); West Bengal Khadi and Village Industries Board; Bishnupur Tantubay Samabay Samity.*

title: How to Store and Care for Your Silk Sarees
excerpt: A silk saree is not just clothing — it is an heirloom. With the right care, it can last three generations. Here is everything you need to know about storing and caring for your silk sarees.
body:
Your grandmother's silk saree, brought out each festival, still holds its lustre. That is not an accident. Silk, when properly cared for, is among the most durable natural fibres on earth. A single silk saree — Kanjivaram, Banarasi, Baluchari — can outlast its owner if stored and maintained correctly.

Here is the complete guide.

## Washing Your Silk Saree

**The golden rule: when in doubt, dry clean.**

For pure silk sarees — particularly those with zari (gold or silver thread) borders — professional dry cleaning is always the safest option. Zari can tarnish and weaken with water, and the dyes in handloom silk are not always water-stable.

**For lighter silks without heavy zari (Tussar, Kosa, Chanderi cotton-silk):**
- Hand wash in cold water only
- Use a mild, pH-neutral detergent — never regular washing powder or bleach
- Do not soak for more than 5 minutes
- Gently swirl — never scrub, wring, or twist
- Rinse twice in cold water; add a teaspoon of white vinegar to the final rinse to restore sheen

**Never put silk in a washing machine**, even on a gentle cycle.

## Drying

- Never wring or tumble dry
- Lay flat on a clean cotton cloth in the shade — **never in direct sunlight**, which fades both natural and chemical dyes
- If you must hang, use a padded hanger and support the entire length
- Allow to dry completely before folding — storing even slightly damp silk causes mildew and weakens the fibre

## Ironing

- Iron on the **reverse side** at a low-to-medium setting (silk setting on your iron)
- Always use a **pressing cloth** between the iron and the fabric, especially over zari and embroidery
- Never iron while the saree is damp — it can stretch the weave
- Do not use steam on silk with heavy zari — moisture causes tarnish

## Removing Stains

Act quickly — the longer a stain sits, the harder it is to remove.

- **Food and oil stains:** blot (do not rub) with a clean white cloth; apply a small amount of mild liquid detergent; rinse with cold water
- **Water stains:** allow to dry completely, then gently rub the stain against itself
- **For anything persistent:** take it to a professional dry cleaner and mention the fabric type and stain source

## Storing Your Silk Sarees

This is where most damage occurs.

**Do:**
- Fold with sheets of muslin or acid-free tissue between each fold to prevent permanent crease lines
- Re-fold along different lines every 3-4 months — the same fold crease weakens the fibre over time
- Store in a cool, dry, well-ventilated cupboard
- Add a neem sachet or dried lavender — natural insect deterrents
- Keep each saree in a separate muslin bag if possible

**Do not:**
- Store in plastic bags or airtight containers — silk needs to breathe
- Stack heavily — the weight compresses the weave
- Store in direct contact with cedar wood — the oils can stain
- Keep with regular cotton or synthetic clothes that carry moisture

## Zari Care

Gold and silver zari borders are particularly delicate.

- Never apply perfume, deodorant, or hairspray near a saree — the chemicals tarnish zari rapidly
- Fold the saree so the zari border is on the inside, protected
- When hanging temporarily, never hang from the zari border
- If your zari has tarnished, a professional silversmith or dry cleaner can sometimes restore it

## When to Seek Help

If you notice:
- A stain that will not lift with gentle home care
- Loose or broken zari threads
- A fraying border or pallu
- Discolouration or mildew spots

...take the saree to a trusted dry cleaner or — better — directly to a weaver or textile restorer. Many weaver communities offer repair and restoration services.

## The Generational Rule

The best-cared-for sarees are aired twice a year, washed only when necessary, never stored in direct sunlight, and treated as what they are — not just garments, but heirlooms. Treat your silk that way and it will outlast you.

---

*Content references: Silk Mark Organisation of India — Silk Care Guidelines (silkmarkindia.com); Central Silk Board, Ministry of Textiles, Government of India (csb.gov.in); Weavers' Service Centre, Kolkata.*

*Amayaa by Polka Dots — Kolkata*

title: Kanjivaram vs Mysore Silk — A Weaver's Perspective
excerpt: Both carry GI tags. Both are pure silk. Both are from South India. But Kanjivaram and Mysore Silk are as different as the cities they come from. A weaver's guide to telling them apart.
body:
Ask a connoisseur to name the two greatest silk sarees of South India and the answer is almost always the same: Kanjivaram and Mysore. Both are pure mulberry silk. Both are GI-protected. Both command respect.

But they are very different sarees — in weight, in structure, in occasion, in spirit.

## Kanjivaram — The Queen of Silks

Kanjivaram silk (also spelled Kanchipuram) comes from the temple town of Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu — a city that has been synonymous with silk weaving for over a thousand years. The craft is believed to have been brought to Kanchipuram by master weavers from Saurashtra in Gujarat, who migrated south under the patronage of the Pallava kings.

**What makes Kanjivaram distinctive:**

Kanjivaram is woven using a special technique where the **body and the border are woven separately** and then interlocked — a technique unique to Kanchipuram. This means the border is structurally integral to the saree, not just stitched on. Run your finger along the border of an authentic Kanjivaram: you will feel the point where the two sections join.

The silk used is triple-twisted mulberry silk — thicker and heavier than most. Zari in Kanjivaram is traditionally made with silver wire coated in gold, though today a range of zari types is used.

**Characteristics of Kanjivaram:**
- Heavy — typically 700g to 900g
- Rich, jewel-toned colours: deep reds, blues, greens, purples
- Bold contrasting borders — often in a completely different colour from the body
- Temple, rudraksham (rudraksha), and peacock motifs dominate
- The pallu features large, prominent motifs — often depicting deities or geometric patterns
- Silk Mark certified; GI protected under GI Tag No. 1 — one of the first GI tags issued in India

A Kanjivaram is the saree of celebration: weddings, temple visits, significant occasions. It makes a statement.

## Mysore Silk — Understated Elegance

Mysore Silk comes from Mysuru (Mysore) in Karnataka. The craft was formally established under the patronage of Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV in the early 20th century — the Mysore Silk Factory, established in 1912, is still operational today and remains one of the primary producers of authentic Mysore silk.

Mysore silk is woven from pure mulberry silk spun in Karnataka's own silk farms — the state is India's largest silk producer, accounting for approximately 45% of the country's total mulberry silk output (Central Silk Board, 2023).

**Characteristics of Mysore Silk:**
- Lighter than Kanjivaram — typically 500g to 650g
- Smooth, almost creamy hand-feel — finer thread count
- Soft, jewel-like colours but more muted than Kanjivaram
- Borders are typically narrower and more subtle
- Motifs are finer, more delicate — florals, checks, stripes
- The sheen is extraordinary — Mysore silk catches light differently at every angle
- GI protected under GI Tag No. 155

Mysore silk is the saree of quiet occasions: formal lunches, cultural events, everyday elegance. It whispers rather than announces.

## Side by Side

| | Kanjivaram | Mysore Silk |
|---|---|---|
| **Origin** | Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu | Mysuru, Karnataka |
| **Weight** | 700–900g (heavy) | 500–650g (lighter) |
| **Texture** | Rich, structured | Smooth, fluid |
| **Border** | Bold, contrasting, interlocked | Subtle, narrower |
| **Motifs** | Temple, rudraksham, large | Fine floral, geometric |
| **Occasion** | Weddings, grand events | Formal, everyday elegance |
| **GI Tag** | No. 1 | No. 155 |

## How to Identify Authentic Kanjivaram

1. **The border join** — run your nail along the inside of the border. Authentic Kanjivaram has a visible ridge where body and border are interlocked.
2. **Weight** — hold the saree. It should feel substantial.
3. **Zari rub test** — rub zari gently against white cloth. Real gold-coated zari leaves no mark; imitation zari leaves a yellow smear.
4. **Silk Mark** — look for the Silk Mark Organisation of India label.

## How to Identify Authentic Mysore Silk

1. **Sheen** — hold up to light. Authentic Mysore silk has an almost luminous sheen unlike any synthetic.
2. **Government label** — authentic Mysore Silk Sarees from the Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation carry a distinct government certification label.
3. **Hand-feel** — it should feel almost buttery. Any roughness indicates blending.

## Which Should You Choose?

Choose **Kanjivaram** if: you want a statement saree for a wedding or major occasion, you love bold colour and grandeur, you want an heirloom that announces its quality.

Choose **Mysore Silk** if: you want something you can wear more often, you prefer understated elegance, you value drape and lightness as much as richness.

At Amayaa by Polka Dots, we carry both — sourced directly from weaver cooperatives and certified units in Kanchipuram and Mysuru.

---

*Content references: Central Silk Board, Ministry of Textiles, Government of India (csb.gov.in) — Annual Report 2022–23; Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation (ksicsilk.com); Geographical Indications Registry, Government of India — GI Tag No. 1 (Kanchipuram Silk) and GI Tag No. 155 (Mysore Silk); Silk Mark Organisation of India (silkmarkindia.com).*

*Amayaa by Polka Dots — Kolkata*

title: How to Drape a Saree — 6 Regional Styles Explained
excerpt: The saree is draped differently in every state of India — each style a reflection of climate, occupation, and culture. Here are six regional draping styles every saree lover should know.
body:
The saree is one garment but not one style. Across India's 28 states, women have developed distinct ways of draping those five to nine yards — each shaped by climate, by religion, by occupation, and by centuries of local culture. Learning these styles does not just expand your wardrobe. It deepens your understanding of India itself.

Here are six regional styles worth knowing — and trying.

## 1. Nivi Drape — Andhra Pradesh & Telangana

**The most common drape in urban India today**

The Nivi drape originated in Andhra Pradesh and spread across India through the influence of nationalist women in the early 20th century — Sarojini Naidu, among others, helped popularise it nationally.

**How it works:**
- The saree is tucked into the petticoat at the front centre, then pleated and tucked again
- The pleats fall cleanly over the left side
- The pallu is draped from the right side, across the front, and over the left shoulder — worn loose and falling down the back

**Best for:** Most silk sarees, formal occasions, first-time draping. If you are learning to drape a saree, start here.

**Pair with:** A fitted blouse; a long or short sleeve works equally well.

## 2. Bengali Drape — West Bengal

**Worn without pleats; the pallu takes centre stage**

The Bengali drape is the traditional style of West Bengal and is especially beautiful with Baluchari, Tant, and Kantha sarees.

**How it works:**
- The saree is wrapped once around the body from right to left
- **No pleats are made at the front** — a key distinction
- The remaining fabric is draped once around the body again, and the pallu is brought over the right shoulder from the back and pinned at the shoulder
- Often a white saree with red border (white Tant with Laal Paar) is worn this way

**Best for:** Tant, Muslin, Baluchari, Kantha sarees. Lightweight fabrics drape most beautifully in this style.

**Pair with:** A short blouse, often with elbow-length sleeves; traditionally no blouse at all was worn, though a fitted short blouse is now standard.

## 3. Gujarati Seedha Pallu — Gujarat & Rajasthan

**The pallu falls in front, not behind**

The Gujarati style is immediately recognisable because the pallu is draped over the **right shoulder**, brought across the front of the body, and pinned at the left shoulder — the reverse of the Nivi drape.

**How it works:**
- Tuck and pleat at the front as in Nivi
- Instead of taking the pallu over the left shoulder, bring it across the front and pin it to the right shoulder at the back
- The pallu then falls over the front — displaying it fully

**Best for:** Bandhani, Patola, heavy zari-bordered sarees where the pallu deserves to be seen.

**Pair with:** A heavily embroidered or mirror-work blouse.

## 4. Maharashtrian Nauvari — Maharashtra

**Nine yards; no petticoat; a dhoti-style drape**

The Nauvari (literally "nine yards") saree is the traditional drape of Maharashtra. It is worn dhoti-style — tucked between the legs, creating divided lower garment — making it ideal for active work, dance (particularly Lavani), and festival occasions.

**How it works:**
- A nine-yard saree is used (not the standard five to six yards)
- The centre of the saree is positioned at the back and the two halves are brought forward
- Pleats are tucked into the front of the waist
- The remaining fabric is tucked between the legs and secured at the back
- The pallu falls over the shoulder in a distinctive style

**Best for:** Paithani, Narayanpet, and traditional cotton sarees. Not suited to heavily starched silks.

**Pair with:** A short front-open blouse (choli); traditionally no blouse at all.

## 5. Coorgi / Kodava Drape — Karnataka

**Pleats at the back; pallu pinned at the front**

The Kodava drape from Coorg (Kodagu) in Karnataka is distinctive and striking — almost the mirror image of a standard drape in where the pleats and pallu fall.

**How it works:**
- The pleats are tucked at the **back** of the waist, not the front
- The saree is wrapped around and the pallu brought over the **right shoulder to the front**, pinned at the right breast
- The overall silhouette is different from Nivi — more structured at the back, flowing at the front

**Best for:** Heavy silks that hold their structure; particularly beautiful in Mysore or Kanjivaram.

**Pair with:** A fitted blouse; often a distinctive Kodava jewellery set with the saree.

## 6. Kerala Mundum Neriyathum — Kerala

**Two-piece; cotton; pure white with gold**

Strictly speaking, the Mundum Neriyathum is not a saree — it is a two-piece garment unique to Kerala. But it is the ancestor of the saree tradition in the south and deserves its place here.

**How it works:**
- The *mundu* (lower cloth) is a single piece wrapped around the lower body in a lungi style and tucked at the waist
- The *neriyathu* (upper cloth) is draped over the left shoulder, across the chest, and often tucked into the waist on the right

**The fabric:** Pure white Kerala cotton or silk with a gold *kasavu* (woven gold) border. The simplicity is the point — the contrast of white and gold is one of the most elegant in Indian textile tradition.

**Best for:** Festivals, temple visits, Onam celebrations.

**Pair with:** A fitted full-sleeved blouse; gold jewellery.

---

## A Note on Learning

Each of these styles takes practice. The best approach is to watch — YouTube has excellent tutorials by weavers and draping experts for each regional style. Once you have learned the Nivi drape, try the Bengali next: removing the pleats changes the character of the saree entirely.

A saree is not just fabric. The way you drape it is a language.
